settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: Expand delegates path construction to FileUtils.resolveFile, which is explicitly documented and tested (FileUtilsTest testResolveFileDot and related tests) as resolving '.'/'..' operators, suggesting normalization is intended and covered by tests.
candidates.description: Expand.expandFile iterates zip entries and passes ze.getName() into extractFile, which computes the output path with FileUtils.resolveFile(dir, entryName) and then writes the entry content to that path (FileOutputStream at line 178). Because the entry name is attacker-influenced (it comes from the zip archive being extracted), the safety of the extraction rests entirely on FileUtils.resolveFile normalizing away '..' traversal and absolute paths. If resolveFile fails to strip all traversal sequences (e.g. via alternate separators or encoded sequences), entry names could resolve outside the destination directory, leading to write-outside-target behavior. I was able to read the extractFile call chain and the write, but not the full body of FileUtils.resolveFile in this review, so I cannot confirm whether normalization is complete.
missing_evidence: Full source of FileUtils.resolveFile (lines around the method body) to confirm whether '..' and absolute names are normalized before File construction
Whether FileUtils.resolveFile canonicalizes the result or only performs lexical normalization
preconditions: Caller invokes Expand.execute()/expandFile with an attacker-supplied zip file
FileUtils.resolveFile does not fully neutralize '..'/absolute entry names (unverified in this review)
candidates.title: Zip entry names from untrusted archives extracted via FileUtils.resolveFile in Expand.extractFile

counter_evidence: The reviewed constructors only perform charset detection and do not themselves parse entities or resolve external DTDs; entity handling would be governed by the XML parser used by the caller, which is outside this class.
candidates.description: XmlReader and its subclass XmlStreamReader accept arbitrary InputStream, File, URL and URLConnection sources and perform charset/encoding sniffing plus lenient detection (doRawStream, doLenientDetection). XmlReader(URL) calls url.openConnection() and XmlReader(URLConnection) inspects content-type headers from a remote source. The lenient path in XmlReader(InputStream, boolean) swallows XmlStreamReaderException when lenient is true and falls back based on message content. These classes read and branch on untrusted data; I looked for but did not find explicit disabling of external entity/DTD resolution in the reviewed ranges, and network connections are opened based on the provided URL. This is reported as an area to verify rather than a confirmed issue.
missing_evidence: How callers configure the underlying XML parser (e.g., security features) is not visible in these files
No explicit DTD/entity configuration appears in the reviewed XmlReader ranges, so absence of a guard cannot be concluded
preconditions: Application constructs XmlReader/XmlStreamReader from attacker-controlled stream, file, or URL
Surrounding parser configuration does not independently disable external entities
candidates.title: Lenient charset detection reads attacker-influenced content and opens URL/URLConnection streams in XmlReader/XmlStreamReader

counter_evidence: The name includes a random value derived from SecureRandom plus freeMemory, increasing unpredictability; javadoc documents that the file is not created, placing responsibility on callers; java.io.tmpdir is typically not world-writable in a way that enables the race on all platforms.
candidates.description: FileUtils.createTempFile builds a candidate name using a Random seeded from SecureRandom plus freeMemory and loops while result.exists(), returning a File without creating it. The returned path is not atomically created, so between the exists() check and a caller's subsequent file creation there is a window in which another process could create the file or a symlink at that path. The javadoc explicitly notes the file is not created by this method. This is a classic predictable-temp-name/TOCTOU pattern, but the name includes a randomized component and the method is a utility that leaves creation to the caller.
missing_evidence: Callers of createTempFile and whether they create the file with exclusive semantics
Actual entropy/observability of rand.nextInt() combined with freeMemory in the deployment environment
preconditions: Caller uses createTempFile and then creates/writes the file trusting the name is unique and safe
An attacker can predict or race the generated name within a shared temp directory
candidates.title: TOCTOU race in FileUtils.createTempFile: existence check without atomic creation

counter_evidence: deleteDirectory first tries directory.delete() to remove symlinked directories before recursing (comment at lines 1611-1613); Java's File.delete does not follow symlinks to delete targets, so symlinked entries are removed as links in typical implementations.
candidates.description: FileUtils.deleteDirectory and cleanDirectory recurse through directory.listFiles() and forceDelete each entry. deleteDirectory attempts directory.delete() first specifically to handle symlinked directories, but cleanDirectory/forceDelete operate on listed entries and call file.delete()/getCanonicalFile() during Windows retry. If a directory tree contains symlinks pointing outside the intended tree, recursive cleaning/deletion could affect targets outside the directory being cleaned, depending on platform symlink semantics.
missing_evidence: Platform-specific behavior of delete on symlinked directories is not verifiable from source alone
Whether callers expose these methods to untrusted directory structures
preconditions: The target directory tree contains symlinks to locations outside it
Caller invokes deleteDirectory/cleanDirectory on a directory that may include attacker-created symlinks
candidates.title: Recursive directory deletion and cleaning follow symlinks via listFiles/delete in FileUtils
